subject: RFI: workload amortization, adaptive batching & cache amortization
messages:
From: Aaron Patel <aaron.patel@globex.com>
To: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.ai>
Cc: Benchmarking Team <benchmarking@globex.com>
Date: Thu, 30 Sep 2026 08:14:00 -0700
Subject: RFI: workload amortization questions for benchmarking

Hi Soojin,

Thanks again for taking our call earlier. As we prepare the RFP technical appendix, the benchmarking committee asked for a focused write-up on how Redwood thinks about amortization of fixed costs (warmup/cache/batch setup) across different workload shapes. Specifically, can you provide:

1) A concise description of how "workload amortization" is computed for inference runs (what is included/excluded).
2) Typical warmup behavior for models hosted on Redwood (cold->steady-state timelines for KV cache, operator JIT, quantization paths) and how you capture that in latency reporting.
3) How adaptive batching interacts with short bursty requests vs long streaming sessions — and the observable impact on p50/p90/p99.
4) Any empirical evidence (graphs or CSV) that show throughput vs sequence-length mix and the batch-amortized per-token cost.

We plan to run a vendor bakeoff next week. If you can send a short narrative + artifacts (CSV with workload matrix + any run commands) that would be great.

Best,
Aaron
Aaron Patel
Sr. MTS, Benchmarking
Globex Corporation

From: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.ai>
To: Aaron Patel <aaron.patel@globex.com>
Cc: marissa.cole@redwood.ai, karthik.iyer@redwood.ai, ben.carter@redwood.ai
Date: Thu, 30 Sep 2026 11:05:00 -0700
Subject: Re: RFI: workload amortization questions for benchmarking

Aaron —

Appreciate the clear list. Attached I’m sending: workload-matrix.csv (your requested sequence-length mixes), batching-latency-graphs.pdf (p50/p90/p99 across mixes), and a small script runbook (runbook-prefill-scripts.sh) to reproduce the key curves on a single Redwood Dedicated pool.

High-level answers up front:
- Workload amortization: we define amortized per-token cost as (total GPU time for the workload + fixed initialization overheads) / total tokens produced. Fixed initialization overheads include model load + initial kernel JIT + cold KV-population pass for the longer contexts. We exclude client-side network RTTs and unrelated infra (e.g., provisioning latency when spinning new nodes beyond autoscaler).
- Warmup behavior: for large open models, cold->steady tends to stabilize within 5–15 seconds of sustained token-generation at moderate batch sizes (depends on sequence length and KV reuse). Cold starts that create new kernels (new seq len path or quantized fallback) show a spike in p99 for the first 1–3 requests. Our reporting provides two lines: cold-primed (first minute) and steady-state (10+ minutes).
- Adaptive batching: the runtime continuously forms bins by seq-length and request age. For short bursty traffic, batching provides modest p50 improvements but p99 can be dominated by head-of-line long requests; we apply short-request-priority windows to bound tail. For long streaming sessions, batching amortizes KV costs effectively and yields better p90/p99.

I’ll loop in Marissa and Karthik to add precise numbers and a suggested benchmarking harness. Are you okay if we include a short canary run manifest that mirrors your expected QPS spike pattern?

Regards,
Soojin Lee
Sr. Solutions Engineer — Redwood Inference

Attachments: workload-matrix.csv (CSV, 12 KB), batching-latency-graphs.pdf (PDF, 380 KB), runbook-prefill-scripts.sh (shell script, 3 KB)

From: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.ai>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 01 Oct 2026 09:20:00 -0700
Subject: Internal: Globex RFI — what to include in methodology notes

Team —

Aaron asked for both narrative and artifacts; he specifically called out amortized per-token cost and warmup timelines. Proposed content to include in the deliverable:

1) Short narrative (1 page) that defines amortization math (I’ll draft).
2) Two sets of latency tables: cold-primed (first 60s) and steady-state (10+min window) across these mixes: 8/64/256/1024 token profiles (we have results in workload-matrix.csv).
3) A disclosure on JIT/quantization warm paths: show example histograms where the first request hits a 3–5× p99 and then drops.
4) Adaptive batching behavior notes: include the short-request-priority window setting (default 30ms) and a recommended knob to tighten to 10ms for Globex if they want lower tail on bursty traffic (cost tradeoff callout).
5) Reproduction steps + exact harness commands (I included runbook-prefill-scripts.sh).

Open questions for engineering:
- Karthik: are the CSV columns enough to show per-model kernel-init times? If not, we should add kernel_init_ms per-run.
- Marissa: can you confirm pricing statement wording around amortized units (we'll avoid promising exact $/token without a committed throughput SLA).

If no objections I’ll send final to Aaron tomorrow EOD PST.

Thanks,
Soojin

From: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.ai>
To: Aaron Patel <aaron.patel@globex.com>
Cc: marissa.cole@redwood.ai, karthik.iyer@redwood.ai
Date: Sat, 02 Oct 2026 10:45:00 -0700
Subject: Re: RFI: workload amortization questions for benchmarking — details and artifacts

Aaron —

Thanks for the patience. Attached are the CSV/graphs and a concise methodology note. Below is a focused summary you can drop into the RFP appendix.

1) Definition: amortized per-token GPU time = (sum over runs of GPU-active-time + fixed-init-overheads) / total tokens. Fixed-init-overheads we include: model binary load (if not pinned), first-kernel JIT passes triggered by new sequence-length buckets, and KV-population passes for long contexts. We explicitly exclude autoscaler provisioning delays and client-side network latency.

2) Warmup behavior (empirical):
- Typical cold->steady: 5–15s for most runs at 8–256 token mixes; ~15–45s for sustained 1024 token runs where KV population dominates.
- Observed p99 spike: initial requests can be 2.5–5× steady p99 if they trigger new kernels or cross quantization fallbacks. See batching-latency-graphs.pdf (pages 2–4).

3) Adaptive batching guidance:
- Default: 30ms short-request window + seq-length binning. This provides best cost-efficiency for mixed workloads.
- For tight tail on bursty workloads: reduce short-request window to 10ms or enable priority lane (recommended for interactive UI workloads). Tradeoff: a ~6–12% increase in amortized per-token GPU cost in our tests at 1k QPS bursts.

4) Empirical artifacts:
- workload-matrix.csv: contains per-run columns: run_id, seq_profile, qps_target, duration_s, gpu_active_ms, kernel_init_ms, tokens_generated.
- batching-latency-graphs.pdf: latency curves across mixes; note the cold-first-minute vs steady-state overlays.
- runbook-prefill-scripts.sh: exact harness commands used to generate the CSV (Docker image tag, Redwood CLI flags for prefill, batch windows).

Reproduction snippet (from runbook):
- docker run --rm redwood/bench:202609 \n  --target-endpoint https://dedicated-us.redwood.ai:443 \n  --model redwood-open-13b-quant \n  --seq-profile "8:0.4,64:0.3,256:0.2,1024:0.1" \n  --qps 300 --duration 900 \n  --prefill-kv true --batch-window-ms 30 \n  --output workload-matrix.csv

Next steps: if you'd like, we can run a short canary with your exact QPS spike pattern (30m run) and provide a bakeoff page in the shared Drive.

Best,
Soojin Lee
Sr. Solutions Engineer — Redwood Inference
soojin.lee@redwood.ai | +1 (415) 555-0198

Attachments: workload-matrix.csv, batching-latency-graphs.pdf, runbook-prefill-scripts.sh
